questions.stem: Which are listed downsides of shivering? Select 2.
questions.explanation: Shivering can sharply increase oxygen demand, creating a particular burden for patients with limited cardiopulmonary reserve. The second keyed effect, increased intracranial pressure, was not independently verified in the inspected passages.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 291

questions.stem: On this graph, which numbered curve fits neuraxial anesthesia?
questions.explanation: Curve 2 continues falling without the plateau seen in curve 1. This fits neuraxial anesthesia, which can prevent the peripheral vasoconstriction needed to conserve core heat.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed pp. 289–290

questions.stem: Why does numbered curve 1 level off?
options: Redistribution reverses back toward the core
Vasoconstriction returns at the lowered threshold
Metabolic rate rises above its baseline
Shivering begins once the core cools
questions.explanation: Thermoregulatory vasoconstriction at the lowered threshold can help produce the plateau in curve 1. The textbook also allows a passive thermal steady state, so the graph alone does not establish a single mechanism.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 289

questions.stem: Combined spinal-general anesthesia is used for a long case. Which curve would you expect, and why?
options: Curve 2, since the block prevents lower-body vasoconstriction
Curve 1, since the block raises the threshold
Neither, since combined techniques prevent hypothermia
questions.explanation: Curve 2 fits continued cooling with combined general and neuraxial anesthesia. The block impairs peripheral vasoconstriction, and the thermoregulatory effects of the two techniques are largely additive.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed pp. 289–290

questions.stem: On this figure, which numbered site is the distal esophagus?
questions.explanation: Site 3 marks the distal end of the illustrated esophageal probe. A properly positioned distal esophageal sensor is a reliable core-temperature site and avoids cooling artifacts from more proximal respiratory gases.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 299

questions.stem: Which numbered sites are core sites? Choose the best set.
questions.explanation: Tympanic membrane, nasopharynx, distal esophagus, and pulmonary arterial blood are core sites in the cited classification. The supplied drawing lacks an anatomical legend, so the complete numbered set 1–4 cannot be independently confirmed from locations alone.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 299

questions.stem: Which numbered site is an intermediate site that is unreliable during rapid thermal changes?
questions.explanation: Rectal and bladder measurements are classified as intermediate sites and may lag during rapid thermal changes. Site 5 appears to represent a pelvic site, but its exact identity and numbered classification need the missing anatomical legend.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 299

questions.stem: Which numbered site would read considerably lower than core temperature?
questions.explanation: Site 7 is drawn on the skin surface rather than in a core compartment. Skin temperature can be considerably lower than core temperature and is strongly affected by peripheral perfusion and the environment.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 299

questions.stem: Which numbered site is most accurate overall for core temperature?
questions.explanation: Pulmonary arterial blood is the reference standard for core-temperature measurement in the cited text. Site 4 appears intended to represent this, but a generic heart-area marker does not independently identify the pulmonary artery without a legend.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 299

questions.stem: Which numbered site is decent for core temperature but carries a bleeding risk?
questions.explanation: Nasopharyngeal temperature can closely reflect core temperature, but probe placement can cause epistaxis, especially with anticoagulation. The risk is source-supported; mapping it specifically to site 2 requires an anatomical legend.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 299

questions.stem: Covering the patient with a blanket mainly reduces which numbered mechanisms?
questions.explanation: Mechanism 2 depicts convection and mechanism 3 depicts radiation. Covering exposed skin reduces both routes of heat loss, with the benefit depending on how much surface is covered.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed pp. 291, 294

questions.stem: A warmed underbody pad addresses which numbered mechanism?
questions.explanation: Mechanism 4 represents conductive heat exchange through contact with the supporting surface. A warmed pad reduces that gradient or transfers heat to the patient, but excessive heat over pressure areas can cause injury.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed pp. 291, 294–295

questions.stem: A patient is prewarmed for 30 minutes. Which numbered phase is most reduced?
questions.explanation: Phase 1 is the early fall in core temperature caused by redistribution into cooler peripheral tissues. Prewarming reduces the core-to-peripheral temperature gradient and therefore limits this initial drop.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 292

questions.stem: A drug raises the slope of segment 2 without moving point 3. What has changed?
questions.explanation: Gain is the magnitude of the change in response per degree of temperature change. A steeper segment 2 with an unchanged threshold at point 3 means increased gain, but “raises the slope” is ambiguous for the downward-sloping line shown.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed pp. 287–288

questions.stem: In a patient at 31°C, which numbered feature would you expect to be prominent?
questions.explanation: Feature 3 marks the T wave in the supplied image, not a clearly shown J wave. The figure and current key therefore do not establish the intended hypothermic ECG finding and require review before this item can be verified.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13 (reading reference only; exact supporting passage not located)

questions.stem: In the colorectal surgery comparison cited in the textbook, perioperative hypothermia approximately tripled the incidence of which complication?
questions.explanation: The cited colorectal-surgery study found approximately threefold higher wound-infection incidence with mild perioperative hypothermia. This is a population-level association, not an exact prediction for an individual finishing at 35.4°C.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 291

questions.stem: Mild hypothermia (35–36°C) significantly increases which transfusion-related outcome?
questions.explanation: Mild hypothermia impairs platelet function and coagulation-enzyme activity, increasing bleeding risk. The cited evidence associates this with a greater need for allogeneic transfusion.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed pp. 287, 291

questions.stem: A patient with a spinal cord injury still shows some reflex thermal responses below the lesion. Why?
options: The hypothalamus extends into the cord
Thermal signals bypass the cord entirely
All thermal processing occurs in the cortex
Some thermal processing occurs in the cord itself
questions.explanation: Although the hypothalamus is the major thermoregulatory integrator, some processing and responses occur within the spinal cord. Thermal regulation is therefore not entirely dependent on an intact pathway to the hypothalamus.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 287

questions.stem: A patient in a 40°C environment with an anticholinergic overdose cannot sweat. Why is this dangerous?
options: Shivering takes over the role sweating usually has
Sweat is the only heat loss route when ambient exceeds core
Vasodilation becomes the main heat-loss route instead
Radiation will still remove most of the heat load
questions.explanation: When the environment is hotter than the body, ordinary dry heat exchange cannot provide the usual outward heat loss. Evaporation of sweat becomes essential, so blocking sweating greatly increases the risk of heat accumulation.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 288

questions.stem: How does active cutaneous vasodilation lower core temperature?
options: It moves heat from the skin into muscle
It increases sweat production from the glands
It diverts blood to the skin, where heat is lost
It reduces metabolic rate in the core organs
questions.explanation: Active cutaneous vasodilation directs more blood to the skin. When the environment permits outward heat transfer, this moves core heat toward the surface for dissipation.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 288

questions.stem: Cutaneous vasoconstriction reduces heat loss through which mechanisms?
options: Convection and radiation from the skin
Conduction into cold IV fluid infusions
Evaporation from the airway and cavities
questions.explanation: Cutaneous vasoconstriction reduces warm blood flow to the skin surface. This limits heat available for loss by radiation and convection.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 288

questions.stem: A 2-month-old under GA is hypothermic. Which heat-production response is impaired by the anesthetic?
questions.explanation: Infants depend heavily on brown-fat nonshivering thermogenesis because shivering is poorly developed. The inspected text establishes that physiology and general anesthetic impairment of thermoregulation, but not the specific suppression claim needed to verify this key.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed pp. 288–289

questions.stem: A PACU patient at 34°C is shivering vigorously. Which complication is most concerning in a patient with coronary disease?
options: A large increase in O2 consumption
questions.explanation: Vigorous shivering can markedly increase oxygen demand. In a patient with coronary disease, that additional demand may exceed the ability to increase myocardial oxygen supply.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 291

questions.stem: Shivering can raise core temperature by about how much per hour?
questions.explanation: Shivering increases metabolic heat production, but the resulting temperature rise depends on heat loss and the patient’s condition. The inspected passage does not verify a fixed rewarming rate of 1.5°C per hour.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 288

questions.stem: Why does GA eliminate the most effective thermoregulatory responses?
questions.explanation: Behavioral responses, such as adding clothing or changing the surroundings, are the strongest thermoregulatory defenses. General anesthesia prevents patients from using these responses.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed pp. 288–289

questions.stem: Thirty minutes after induction, core temp has fallen 1.2°C, but heat content of the body has changed little. Why?
options: The probe moved to a peripheral site
Heat was lost by radiation to the cold room
Heat moved core to periphery, not out of the body
questions.explanation: Anesthetic vasodilation allows heat to move from the warm core into cooler peripheral tissues. Core temperature can therefore fall substantially before there is a comparable change in total body heat content.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed pp. 289, 292

questions.stem: During the linear phase under GA, temperature falls because heat loss exceeds:
questions.explanation: During the slower linear phase, heat continues to leave the body faster than metabolism replaces it. This ongoing heat imbalance differs from the initial redistribution phase.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 289

questions.stem: Which change in thresholds best describes GA's effect on thermoregulation?
options: No threshold changes; only the gain changes
Cold and warm thresholds both rise sharply
Warm thresholds fall while cold thresholds rise
Cold thresholds fall; sweating threshold barely moves
questions.explanation: General anesthetics substantially lower the thresholds for vasoconstriction and shivering while having relatively little effect on the sweating threshold. The enlarged interthreshold range permits greater temperature drift without a corrective response.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 289

questions.stem: A high spinal (T4) and a low spinal (T10) are compared. Which impairs thermoregulation more?
questions.explanation: A higher neuraxial block impairs thermoregulatory control over a greater region. Because the effect scales with dermatomal block height, the T4 block is expected to impair regulation more than the T10 block.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 289

questions.stem: Neuraxial anesthesia impairs which behavioral response?
options: Patients request more blankets than needed
Patients may not feel or report being cold
Patients shiver vigorously below the block
questions.explanation: Neuraxial anesthesia can reduce the perception of cold and the discomfort that normally prompts protective behavior. Patients may therefore fail to report being cold even while hypothermic.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 289

questions.stem: Why may a patient under spinal anesthesia need a core temperature probe even though awake and comfortable?
options: Spinals enhance shivering below the block
They can be hypothermic without feeling cold
Spinals raise core temperature during surgery
Awake patients can’t be actively warmed
questions.explanation: Comfort does not reliably exclude hypothermia during neuraxial anesthesia because cold perception and thermoregulatory defenses are impaired. Temperature measurement can detect cooling that the awake patient does not notice.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 289

questions.stem: Which heat-loss route rises most when the room is cold and the patient is uncovered?
questions.explanation: Radiation is the largest route of environmental heat loss in the cited perioperative description. A colder room and more exposed skin increase the opportunity for radiative heat loss.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed pp. 290–291

questions.stem: A cold infusion lowers temperature mainly through which mechanism?
questions.explanation: Cold infused fluid receives heat directly from the patient’s blood and tissues. The text classifies this direct transfer as conductive heat loss.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 291

questions.stem: Which change reduces evaporative heat loss from the respiratory tract?
options: Removing the HME to lower resistance
questions.explanation: Low fresh-gas flows and retained humidity reduce the heat and water needed to condition inspired gas. This limits respiratory evaporative heat loss, although that route contributes relatively little to adult total heat loss.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed pp. 292–293

questions.stem: A trauma patient at 34.5°C is bleeding with normal PT/PTT. Which intervention addresses the coagulopathy most directly?
options: Giving more crystalloid at room temperature
questions.explanation: Hypothermia can impair platelet function and coagulation-enzyme activity, and correcting temperature addresses that mechanism. The inspected passage does not establish the normal-PT/PTT testing nuance in this scenario, so the complete clinical claim remains flagged.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 291

questions.stem: Hypothermic platelet dysfunction is best described as:
questions.explanation: Hypothermia impairs platelet aggregation without necessarily destroying platelets. The cited text describes this dysfunction as reversible, making restoration of normothermia relevant to correcting it.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 291

questions.stem: Why can perioperative hypothermia increase blood pressure and heart rate?
questions.explanation: Hypothermia is associated with increased plasma catecholamines and elevations in heart rate and blood pressure. These changes can increase cardiac stress rather than reflecting a protective fall in metabolic demand.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 291

questions.stem: How does hypothermia impair immune defense at the wound?
options: Vasoconstriction lowers wound O2; immunity is impaired
Cold improves antibiotic penetration at the wound
Vasodilation floods the wound with skin bacteria
questions.explanation: Cold-induced vasoconstriction reduces oxygen delivery to the wound. Hypothermia also directly impairs immune function and tissue healing, increasing infection risk.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 291

questions.stem: A patient cools from 37 to 35.5°C during a liver resection. Which change in blood loss would you anticipate?
questions.explanation: Mild hypothermia is associated with increased bleeding and transfusion risk. The inspected passage does not support predicting an additional 500 mL of blood loss for this liver-resection scenario.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 291

questions.stem: A patient at 35°C has a slow recovery from rocuronium. What is the explanation?
options: Sugammadex works less well when warm
questions.explanation: Hypothermia prolongs the action of neuromuscular blockers by reducing drug metabolism and delaying hepatic or renal clearance. Rocuronium recovery can therefore be slower, requiring assessment of actual neuromuscular recovery rather than elapsed time alone.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 12, printed p. 171

questions.stem: With hypothermia, how should volatile agent dosing change?
questions.explanation: Hypothermia decreases MAC, indicating a reduced concentration requirement for immobility under comparable conditions. Volatile-agent dosing should therefore be reassessed as temperature falls rather than automatically increased.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 7, printed p. 81

questions.stem: Which renal effect of hypothermia is listed?
questions.explanation: Cold diuresis is the current keyed answer. A passage establishing this renal effect was not located in the inspected textbook material, so the answer remains unverified rather than being assigned a guessed page.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13 (reading reference only; exact supporting passage not located)

questions.stem: Which metabolic abnormality is on Wolpaw's hypothermia list?
questions.explanation: The current key selects hypoglycemia, but a supporting passage for that generalization was not located. Glucose abnormalities require clinical context, so this item needs a specific source and answer review.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13 (reading reference only; exact supporting passage not located)

questions.stem: The J wave appears where on the ECG?
options: In the middle of the PR interval
questions.explanation: The keyed choice places the J wave immediately after the QRS complex. The inspected temperature material does not verify this ECG detail, so the item still needs a specific supporting passage.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13 (reading reference only; exact supporting passage not located)

questions.stem: Hyperthermia increases cardiovascular stress mainly through which mechanism?
questions.explanation: Hyperthermia increases metabolic demand and places additional stress on the cardiovascular system. Greater oxygen and circulatory requirements explain why a substantial temperature rise can be hazardous.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 292

questions.stem: Which pattern most suggests MH rather than overwarming?
options: Slow rise late in a long case under full warming
Flushed skin with a normal, stable EtCO2
Rapid temp rise with tachycardia and rising EtCO2
questions.explanation: Rapidly increasing CO₂ together with tachycardia and a rising temperature raises concern for a hypermetabolic crisis such as malignant hyperthermia. Simple overwarming alone does not adequately explain the combined pattern, but clinical confirmation and differential assessment remain necessary.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 292

questions.stem: During a prolonged procedure, which adjustment can help prevent excessive warming?
options: Lower the Bair Hugger as needed
Use only passive blankets from the start
questions.explanation: Temperature monitoring allows active warming to be reduced or stopped as needed. The cited text identifies excessive warming as a common cause of intraoperative hyperthermia and recommends discontinuing it when overheating occurs.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 292

questions.stem: A patient on haloperidol for 3 days develops lead-pipe rigidity, fever, and labile BP. Which treatment is listed?
options: Restart haloperidol at a lower dose
Stop the drug, supportive care, and dantrolene
questions.explanation: Antipsychotic exposure can be associated with neuroleptic malignant syndrome, a drug-related hyperthermic disorder. The full keyed treatment combination, including dantrolene, was not independently verified in the inspected passages and needs a specific treatment source.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 14, printed p. 215; Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 292

questions.stem: A Parkinson's patient's levodopa is held for 2 days before surgery. Fever, rigidity, and confusion develop. What is the likely diagnosis and first step?
questions.explanation: The key proposes a neuroleptic-malignant-like syndrome after interruption of dopaminergic therapy and restarting that therapy. Neither the specific withdrawal diagnosis nor the complete management step was independently verified in the inspected passages.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13 (reading reference only; exact supporting passage not located)

questions.stem: Which drug combination in the OR could precipitate serotonin syndrome in a patient on an SSRI?
questions.explanation: SSRIs, fentanyl, and methylene blue are among the agents implicated in serotonin toxicity in the cited text. Combining serotonergic exposures can increase risk, although the presence of the drugs alone does not diagnose the syndrome.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 14, printed pp. 213–214

questions.stem: Which neuromuscular finding is characteristic of serotonin syndrome?
questions.explanation: Clonus is a characteristic neuromuscular sign of serotonin toxicity. It is central to the Hunter criteria and is more informative here than isolated fasciculations or flaccid paralysis.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 14, printed pp. 213–214

questions.stem: Which treatment helps NMS but not serotonin syndrome?
questions.explanation: The inspected serotonin-toxicity discussion supports stopping implicated drugs, supportive care, and syndrome-specific treatment. It does not independently establish the keyed comparison that dantrolene helps NMS but not serotonin syndrome.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 14, printed pp. 213–215

questions.stem: Why is redistribution hypothermia difficult to prevent once anesthesia starts?
options: The OR is always kept too cold to prevent it
Vasodilation moves core heat out to the periphery
Metabolic rate doubles right at induction
Warming devices can’t be used after induction
questions.explanation: Induction-related vasodilation allows warm core blood to mix with cooler peripheral tissues. Surface warming begun after induction cannot instantly remove that preexisting temperature gradient, so preventing the early redistribution drop is difficult.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed pp. 289, 292

questions.stem: Prewarming works by increasing what?
questions.explanation: Prewarming increases peripheral heat content and narrows the temperature difference between core and peripheral tissues. Less heat therefore redistributes away from the core after anesthetic vasodilation.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 292

questions.stem: A trauma patient receives 4 L of room-temperature crystalloid. Approximately how much could mean body temperature fall?
questions.explanation: The cited example estimates about a 0.25°C fall per liter of room-temperature crystalloid. Four liters could therefore contribute roughly a 1°C fall under comparable assumptions, with the actual change depending on other heat inputs and losses.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed pp. 291, 293

questions.stem: Which product has a similar cooling effect to a liter of room-temperature crystalloid?
options: One unit of platelets at room temperature
questions.explanation: The text describes a liter of crystalloid and a unit of refrigerated packed red cells as potentially important cooling loads. Their effects depend on product temperature and volume, which is why rapid fluid or blood administration may require warming.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 293

questions.stem: For which types of surgery does the textbook describe raising the operating-room temperature as a usual practice?
questions.explanation: A warmer operating room reduces the gradient driving environmental heat loss. The cited text specifically describes this practice during liver transplantation and major trauma.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 294

questions.stem: Raising OR temperature mainly reduces which mechanism?
questions.explanation: Raising room temperature reduces the temperature difference between the patient and surrounding surfaces. This decreases radiative heat loss, a major route of intraoperative heat loss.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 294

questions.stem: Warm cotton blankets reduce which types of heat loss?
options: Conduction into the OR table only
questions.explanation: Cotton blankets insulate covered skin and reduce radiative, convective, and evaporative heat loss. They primarily conserve heat rather than actively increase body temperature.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 294

questions.stem: How do forced-air warmers add heat to the patient?
questions.explanation: Forced-air systems move warmed air through a blanket over the patient. Heat is transferred to the covered skin primarily by convection.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 295

questions.stem: According to the cited textbook, which warming system was most commonly used perioperatively in the United States?
questions.explanation: The cited textbook describes forced-air warming as the most commonly employed method in the United States. That statement is specific to the text’s setting and does not establish a universal or current worldwide ranking.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 295

questions.stem: A patient is placed on an underbody warming pad set high. What risk does Wolpaw's explanation imply?
options: Burns, since compressed tissue sheds heat poorly
More evaporative loss from the patient’s back
questions.explanation: Compressed tissue beneath a patient may have reduced blood flow and less ability to dissipate applied heat. Excessive heating in these pressure areas can therefore cause thermal injury.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 295

questions.stem: Per the rewarming table, which technique is best for HT I (mild hypothermia)?
options: Warm room, clothing, and active movement
questions.explanation: Clothing, activity, and a warm environment are behavioral ways to conserve or generate heat. The specified HT I rewarming table was not located in the supplied passages, so its stage-specific recommendation remains unverified.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed pp. 288, 294

questions.stem: For HT IV when ECMO or CPB isn't available, which technique does the table list?
questions.explanation: The current key selects thoracic lavage as a fallback for HT IV when extracorporeal support is unavailable. The specific staged-rewarming table and this treatment indication were not located in the inspected texts.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13 (reading reference only; exact supporting passage not located)

questions.stem: Which rewarming technique in the table has an "uncertain" indication at about 2–4°C/hr?
questions.explanation: The keyed hemodialysis indication and 2–4°C-per-hour rate depend on the referenced table. That table was not located, so neither the exact rate nor its stated indication is verified.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13 (reading reference only; exact supporting passage not located)

questions.stem: Why are thermistor esophageal probes preferred in the OR?
options: They need no placement below the larynx
Accurate, cheap, stable, and at a core site
They detect fever trends but not values
questions.explanation: Thermistors are inexpensive, stable electronic temperature sensors with reproducible readings. An appropriately placed distal esophageal probe combines those properties with a reliable core measurement site.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed pp. 296, 299

questions.stem: Liquid crystal thermometers work because cholesteric crystals do what?
questions.explanation: Cholesteric liquid crystals change their optical properties and color with temperature. Their surface readings can differ substantially from core temperature, especially during rapid changes.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 298

questions.stem: Core temperature sites are reliable even under which conditions?
questions.explanation: Pulmonary arterial blood, distal esophagus, tympanic membrane, and nasopharynx track core temperature closely when correctly measured. The cited classification regards these sites as reliable even during major thermal changes, unlike intermediate sites that may lag.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 299

questions.stem: The temperature regulating center receives signals from where?
options: Peripheral receptors in the skin only
questions.explanation: Thermoregulatory control integrates input from peripheral skin receptors and central structures. The hypothalamus is the principal integrator, but it is not the only source or processing site.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed pp. 287–288

questions.stem: A patient has a postoperative temperature of 38.4°C on day 1. Per Wolpaw's facts, what is TRUE?
options: Most postop fevers are from wound infection
Fever above 38°C should always be treated
Most postop fevers are not from infection
questions.explanation: Postoperative temperature elevation can have multiple causes and must be interpreted in context. The inspected passage does not verify that most day-one postoperative fevers are noninfectious, so the keyed frequency claim remains unresolved.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 292

questions.stem: Treating fever below what temperature may cause harm per Wolpaw?
questions.explanation: The current key specifies 40°C, but a supporting passage for that treatment-harm threshold was not located. This numerical clinical claim should not be applied or presented as textbook-verified without its exact source.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13 (reading reference only; exact supporting passage not located)

questions.stem: Which patient is at greatest risk for unintended hypothermia?
options: Adult under forced-air warming for a short case
Young adult under sedation for a brief procedure
Elderly patient with extensive burns in a long case
questions.explanation: Advanced age, prolonged surgery, and extensive burns are all listed risk factors for unintended hypothermia. The elderly patient with extensive burns in a long operation combines these risks.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 291

questions.stem: Postoperative shivering raises O2 demand by up to 468%. Which patient needs prevention most?
options: Patient with severe coronary artery disease
questions.explanation: Shivering can greatly increase oxygen demand, with the cited range reaching 468%. A patient with severe coronary disease has limited reserve to meet that demand and is therefore particularly vulnerable among these choices.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 291

questions.stem: Which outcome measure does Wolpaw attach to a temperature of 35°C?
questions.explanation: Hypothermia-related infection, slower drug clearance, and delayed recovery can prolong hospital stay. The exact additional 2.5 days attached to 35°C was not established in the inspected passage.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 291

questions.stem: Which anesthetic drug classes can impair thermoregulatory control?
options: Volatile anesthetics only, not IV agents
questions.explanation: Volatile agents, nitrous oxide, propofol, and opioids can all impair thermoregulatory control. Their important effects include lowering vasoconstriction and shivering thresholds.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 289

questions.stem: Why may the temperature decline continue indefinitely under neuraxial alone?
options: Vasoconstriction is blocked, so no plateau forms
questions.explanation: Neuraxial blockade impairs peripheral vasoconstriction, so the normal plateau may be absent during surgery. The source does not establish that cooling must continue indefinitely or that a plateau can never occur.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 290

questions.stem: Which is NOT a listed consequence of hyperthermia?
questions.explanation: Hyperthermia increases metabolic demand rather than decreasing it. The cited complications include coagulopathy, renal and liver dysfunction, and seizures.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 292

questions.stem: A severely hypothermic patient with cardiac instability is warming 2°C/hr with forced air. Which escalation offers the fastest rate per the table?
questions.explanation: Cardiopulmonary bypass can actively rewarm blood through a heat exchanger and can be used in profound hypothermia. The referenced table’s fastest-rate comparison and the scenario’s forced-air rate were not independently verified.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 295

questions.stem: Prewarming is started 15 minutes before induction. Based on both lectures, what should you expect?
options: No benefit, because prewarming needs at least 30 minutes
Partial benefit; Wolpaw cites 2 hours for full effect
questions.explanation: Prewarming reduces the core-to-peripheral gradient, but its effect depends on duration, heat delivery, and patient factors. The source includes 30-minute prewarming evidence and does not verify a universal two-hour requirement or the exact 15-minute prediction in the key.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 292

questions.stem: Which statement about shivering's efficiency is TRUE?
options: Heat production rises 50–100% at a large O2 cost
It is the most efficient thermoregulatory response
It decreases O2 consumption while adding heat
It is fully functional in newborns and infants
questions.explanation: Shivering can increase metabolic heat production by 50–100%, but it also imposes a substantial oxygen demand. It is not the strongest overall thermoregulatory defense, and it is poorly developed in newborns.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed pp. 288, 291

questions.stem: Why is the distal esophagus favored over the proximal esophagus?
options: Proximal readings are more stable during surgery
It reflects blood temp near the heart, not airway gas
Distal placement keeps the probe out of the stomach
Proximal readings are always higher than core
questions.explanation: The distal esophagus gives a reliable core-temperature estimate and is less affected by cooling from respiratory gases in the trachea. A more proximal probe can therefore be less representative of core temperature.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 299

questions.stem: A thermistor probe reads 34.9°C. Given its accuracy, the true value is most likely within:
questions.explanation: Using the text’s approximate ±0.2°C thermistor accuracy, 34.9°C corresponds to about 34.7–35.1°C. This assumes a functioning, correctly placed sensor; sensor accuracy does not remove site or placement error.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 296

questions.stem: Evaporation from the respiratory tract is part of which share of heat loss?
questions.explanation: The cited 8–10% evaporative share includes water loss from the respiratory tract and open body cavities. It is distinct from radiative or convective heat loss.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 291

questions.stem: Which statements about bellows are correct? Select 3.
options: Descending bellows can hide a disconnect
Descending bellows collapse with a disconnect
The ascending bellows spill valve adds a little PEEP
Ascending bellows entrain room air on disconnect
questions.explanation: Ascending bellows rise during expiration and may fail to refill when the circuit is disconnected, while descending bellows can continue moving by drawing in room air. The standing-bellows relief-valve design also commonly adds a small amount of PEEP.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 160; Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed pp. 275–276

questions.stem: Which are features of piston ventilators? Select 3.
questions.explanation: The described piston ventilators use an electric motor and fresh-gas decoupling. In the cited design, relief valves open near +75 ± 5 and −8 cmH₂O; these are model-specific values, not guaranteed settings for every piston ventilator.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 276

questions.stem: Peak inspiratory pressure rises while plateau pressure is unchanged. Which causes are consistent with this pattern? Select three.
questions.explanation: A rise in peak pressure with unchanged plateau pressure suggests increased flow resistance rather than a new elastic load. A kinked tube, mucus plug, and bronchospasm all fit that mechanism during comparable volume-controlled breaths.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 152, 166; Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 277

questions.stem: Which changes can result from lengthening expiratory time? Select three.
questions.explanation: Longer expiration can reduce incomplete emptying, intrinsic PEEP, and the hemodynamic burden of prolonged positive pressure. Better CO₂ clearance is conditional on effective alveolar ventilation, so the complete three-answer set is not independently verified.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 160, 163; Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 29, printed p. 644

questions.stem: Which pairings of mode and variable are correct? Select 2.
questions.explanation: In volume control, the set volume is targeted while pressure varies with resistance and compliance. In pressure control, inspiratory pressure is targeted while tidal volume varies with respiratory mechanics and other settings.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 166

questions.stem: Which favor pressure control? Select 3.
options: Normal lungs in a short supine case
Need for a fixed tidal volume
questions.explanation: Pressure control can be useful when limiting pressure or accommodating a leak is important, such as in neonates or with an uncuffed tube. It may also help in low-compliance conditions, including adverse positioning, while delivered volume still requires monitoring.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed pp. 277–278

questions.stem: Which are risks of high PEEP? Select 3.
questions.explanation: Excessive PEEP can impair venous return and cause hypotension, while overdistension increases injury risk. The additional keyed intracranial-pressure effect needs a specific supporting passage before the complete set can be verified.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 159, 164

questions.stem: Which are benefits of SIMV? Select 3.
options: Full Vt on every spontaneous breath
questions.explanation: SIMV times mandatory breaths around patient activity and can reduce breath stacking. A fixed minimum minute volume depends on mode, delivered tidal volume, and system integrity, so the unqualified guarantee in the key needs review.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 169; Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 278

questions.stem: Which are risks of recruitment maneuvers? Select 3.
options: Loss of recruited lung when switching to the vent
questions.explanation: Recruitment uses increased airway pressure to reopen lung units, bringing potential overdistension and hemodynamic effects. The inspected passages do not verify the entire three-part risk set, particularly loss of recruitment during the specified switch to the ventilator.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 159; Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 277

questions.stem: Which are effects of setting trigger sensitivity too high (hard to trigger)? Select 2.
questions.explanation: A difficult trigger requires greater inspiratory effort before assistance begins. Weak efforts may fail to meet the threshold, increasing patient work and producing missed assisted breaths.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 278

questions.stem: Which panel shows an ascending (standing) bellows?
questions.explanation: Panel A shows the bellows moving upward during filling, the characteristic ascending or standing design. Bellows classification refers to their movement during expiration.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 160

questions.stem: Which panel's bellows can keep moving normally despite a circuit disconnection?
questions.explanation: Panel B shows a descending or hanging bellows. It can draw room air and continue filling after disconnection, so apparent bellows movement does not establish an intact patient circuit.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 160

questions.stem: Mid-case, the bellows in panel A stays partly collapsed at end-expiration. FIRST check?
questions.explanation: An ascending bellows should refill during expiration. Failure to return to its normal filled position raises concern for a leak or disconnection and requires prompt assessment of the patient and circuit.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 160; Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 277

questions.stem: On this piston system, which numbered component is the fresh gas decoupling valve?
questions.explanation: Component 2 is the fresh-gas decoupling valve in the supplied schematic. Closing it during inspiration diverts fresh gas away from the delivered tidal volume and toward the reservoir bag.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed pp. 280–281

questions.stem: During inspiration, fresh gas from numbered point 3 collects in which numbered component?
questions.explanation: During inspiration, fresh gas is diverted to the manual reservoir bag, shown as component 4. This prevents its continuing flow from augmenting the piston-delivered tidal volume.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 280

questions.stem: During expiration, which numbered component is refilled with fresh gas?
questions.explanation: Component 1 is the piston unit, which refills during expiration. Its refill includes exhaled gas and fresh gas stored in the reservoir bag through the reopened decoupling pathway.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 280

questions.stem: Numbered component 4 develops a large leak during mechanical ventilation. Which problem is most likely?
options: Higher tidal volume from the extra fresh gas
Room air entrainment and agent dilution
questions.explanation: A fresh-gas-decoupled piston system depends on the reservoir bag during refill, and the text warns of possible negative pressure and room-air dilution. The exact consequence and priority for a large leak in component 4 require a device-specific passage or manual.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed pp. 276, 280–281

questions.stem: Which panel shows volume-controlled ventilation?
questions.explanation: Panel A shows constant inspiratory flow with rising airway pressure. This is the illustrated volume-control pattern.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 166–167

questions.stem: In panel B, which variable is held constant during inspiration?
questions.explanation: Panel B maintains inspiratory airway pressure while flow decreases as the lungs fill. Tidal volume varies rather than being the fixed variable.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 166–167

questions.stem: In panel A, compliance falls suddenly. What changes on the waveforms?
options: Tidal volume falls; pressure is unchanged
Peak pressure rises; flow is unchanged
questions.explanation: At unchanged tidal volume and flow, lower compliance requires more elastic inflation pressure. Peak pressure rises while the selected flow is maintained.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 152, 166

questions.stem: In panel B, compliance falls suddenly. What changes?
options: Flow decays faster; tidal volume falls
Peak pressure rises sharply each breath
questions.explanation: At unchanged pressure and resistance in a passive lung model, reduced compliance shortens filling and reduces delivered volume. Flow falls toward zero sooner while the pressure target remains unchanged.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 152, 166

questions.stem: Which pressure trace panel shows controlled (mandatory) ventilation?
questions.explanation: Panel A shows regular machine-delivered pulses without a preceding negative patient-effort deflection. This fits controlled mandatory ventilation in the schematic.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 166–168

questions.stem: Which panel shows patient-triggered breaths that receive full machine support?
questions.explanation: Panel B has a small negative pressure deflection before each full supported breath. This indicates patient effort triggering machine assistance.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 168

questions.stem: Which panel shows mandatory breaths with spontaneous breaths in between?
questions.explanation: Panel C combines large mandatory breaths with smaller spontaneous efforts between them. This is the intermittent mandatory ventilation pattern shown in the text.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 169

questions.stem: Which panel shows spontaneous breathing around a single elevated baseline pressure?
questions.explanation: Panel D shows spontaneous breaths fluctuating around one elevated pressure baseline. This is consistent with CPAP rather than separate mandatory pressure pulses.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 170

questions.stem: Which flow-time panel shows a 1:1 I:E ratio?
questions.explanation: Panel A gives approximately equal time to inspiration and expiration. Its timing therefore corresponds to an I:E ratio near 1:1.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 153–154

questions.stem: Which panel best suits a patient with severe COPD?
questions.explanation: Panel C provides the longest expiratory interval among the diagrams. Extra expiratory time helps obstructed lungs empty and reduces air trapping.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 29, printed p. 644

questions.stem: Which panel matches the mechanical ventilation default I:E ratio?
questions.explanation: Panel B gives approximately one part inspiration to two parts expiration. The text describes 1:2 as a typical initial adult setting rather than a universal device default.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 277

questions.stem: Switching from panel B to panel A changes which of the following?
options: Lowers mean airway pressure and raises expiratory time
Raises mean airway pressure and lowers expiratory time
questions.explanation: Moving from B to A increases the inspiratory fraction and shortens expiration. Mean airway pressure may rise, but that part of the key depends on settings absent from the flow-only figure.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 153–154, 160

questions.stem: A patient has a tidal volume of 500 mL, inspiratory flow of 50 L/min, resistance of 10 cm H₂O/(L/s), compliance of 50 mL/cm H₂O, and PEEP of 5 cm H₂O. What is the approximate peak inspiratory pressure?
questions.explanation: Elastic pressure is 500/50 = 10 cmH₂O, while resistive pressure is (50/60) × 10 = 8.3 cmH₂O. Adding PEEP gives approximately 23.3 cmH₂O for the passive constant-flow model.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 152

questions.stem: Assuming end-inspiratory alveolar pressure equals tidal volume divided by compliance plus PEEP, what is the pressure for a tidal volume of 600 mL, compliance of 40 mL/cm H₂O, and PEEP of 5 cm H₂O?
questions.explanation: Elastic pressure is 600/40 = 15 cmH₂O. Adding 5 cmH₂O PEEP gives approximately 20 cmH₂O at zero flow in the stated model.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 152

questions.stem: Compliance halves while Vt and PEEP stay the same. What happens to the volume/compliance term?
questions.explanation: At fixed tidal volume, the elastic pressure term is V/C. Halving compliance doubles that term, while PEEP and resistive pressure remain separate components.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 152

questions.stem: Ventilator drive mechanisms are classified as:
questions.explanation: Bellows, piston, and turbine describe how the ventilator moves or pressurizes breathing gas. Power source and cycling criteria are separate classifications.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 160–162

questions.stem: Triggering can be by time or by spontaneous effort sensed as:
questions.explanation: A breath can start after a set interval or after detection of patient effort. Pressure, volume, or flow changes can provide that effort signal, depending on the ventilator.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 162

questions.stem: Why can a gas-driven anesthesia ventilator require electrical power even when compressed gas drives its bellows?
options: Electrical circuits and solenoid valves control its operation
The driving gas must be electrically heated
Bellows cannot move without an electric motor
The electrical outlet supplies the driving-gas pressure
questions.explanation: A bag-in-a-bottle anesthesia ventilator can use compressed gas to move the bellows while electrical circuits and solenoids control its operation. Some transport ventilators operate solely on pneumatic power, so electricity is not universally required.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 160; Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 275

questions.stem: Which ventilator component maintains and controls positive airway pressure such as PEEP?
questions.explanation: An expiratory control valve regulates outflow to maintain positive end-expiratory pressure. Its function differs from gas blending or opening the inspiratory pathway.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 174–175

questions.stem: A machine with ascending bellows shows PEEP of 3 cmH2O with PEEP set to zero. Why?
options: The piston adds a small PEEP
The APL adds PEEP in vent mode
The spill valve adds baseline PEEP
questions.explanation: The standing-bellows spill valve stays closed until the bellows fills, creating baseline PEEP. The described design commonly produces about 2–3 cmH₂O before additional selected PEEP.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 275

questions.stem: Why do newer descending bellows machines need extra disconnect alarms?
options: Drive gas leaks into the patient
Bellows can fill from room air
questions.explanation: Descending bellows can continue filling from room air after disconnection. Visible bellows movement alone therefore cannot confirm an intact patient circuit.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 160

questions.stem: A bellows leak causes higher than expected airway pressures. Why?
options: Driving gas pressure enters the circuit
questions.explanation: A tear can connect the high-pressure driving-gas space to the patient circuit. This may transmit excess pressure and dilute the intended breathing-gas mixture.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 160–161

questions.stem: In an ascending bellows leak, agent dilution happens mainly during which phase?
questions.explanation: A bellows leak can mix driving gas with patient gas and dilute anesthetic concentration. The inspected passage does not establish expiration as the principal dilution phase.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 160–161

questions.stem: Why does a piston ventilator need a separate pop-off (relief) valve?
options: Its rigid chamber could build excess pressure
It runs on compressed driving gas from the pipeline
It has no reservoir bag in the circuit
It has no expiratory valve at all
questions.explanation: A piston can pressurize gas within its rigid chamber. A positive-pressure relief pathway protects against excessive pressure rather than supplying driving gas.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 276

questions.stem: What is the purpose of the piston's negative pressure relief valve opening at −8 cmH2O?
options: Add a small amount of PEEP
Admit room air to limit negative pressure
Release excess fresh gas to the scavenger
questions.explanation: The negative-pressure relief valve admits room air when circuit pressure becomes sufficiently negative. The cited approximately −8 cmH₂O threshold is specific to the described piston design.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 276

questions.stem: A patient makes vigorous inspiratory efforts against a piston ventilator with low FGF. Which risk rises?
options: Fresh gas overload in the bag
Relief valve opening with room air entry
Barotrauma from the compressed driving gas
questions.explanation: Strong effort with inadequate circuit gas can generate negative pressure. The relief pathway may then admit room air and dilute the intended gas mixture.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 276, 281

questions.stem: Why is fresh gas decoupling a benefit for low-flow anesthesia?
options: It raises fresh gas flow automatically
Vt stays consistent as fresh gas changes
questions.explanation: Fresh-gas decoupling prevents continuous fresh-gas flow from adding to the ventilator-delivered volume. This helps preserve tidal volume as fresh-gas flow changes.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 280

questions.stem: During an O2 pipeline failure, which machine design lets mechanical ventilation continue without consuming the cylinder for drive gas?
questions.explanation: An electrically driven piston does not require compressed oxygen for its driving force. Ventilation can continue without spending cylinder oxygen to drive bellows, provided electricity and a safe breathing-gas supply remain available.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 276

questions.stem: Why might you fail to notice a piston ventilator stop cycling?
options: It is louder than a bellows
It is quiet and may not be visible
questions.explanation: Piston movement may be hidden and cycling may be quiet. Alarms and measured ventilation are therefore more dependable than audible or visible motion alone.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 276

questions.stem: During expiration, what does a turbine do?
options: Slows to maintain PEEP and low flows
questions.explanation: The described turbine reduces speed during expiration while continuing to spin. Together with the pressure-control valve, this permits exhalation while maintaining intended circuit pressure.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 177

questions.stem: Solenoid valves help regulate which ventilator functions?
options: Gas mixing, Vt timing, and pressure
questions.explanation: Solenoid valves open and close gas pathways with precise electronic timing. They help regulate flow, delivered volume, and circuit pressure rather than absorber chemistry.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 162

questions.stem: Default flow-cycling is set similar to calm, awake ventilation at about:
questions.explanation: Flow cycling ends inspiration at a selected flow criterion, often a fraction of peak flow. The inspected passages do not establish 5 L/min as a universal default or calm-awake reference.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 162, 168

questions.stem: Volume-cycled ventilators carry a higher risk of what?
questions.explanation: Excessive volume or pressure can overdistend alveoli and cause barotrauma. Volume cycling alone does not establish higher comparative risk without specifying delivered volume, pressure limits, and the comparison mode.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 159

questions.stem: During laser airway surgery, which inspired oxygen approach reduces fire risk while maintaining adequate oxygenation?
options: Lowest FiO2 that keeps SpO2 acceptable
questions.explanation: Oxygen supports combustion, so an airway ignition source requires limiting oxygen concentration while preserving adequate oxygenation. Neither fixed high oxygen nor room air regardless of saturation is an appropriate universal rule.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 8, printed p. 211

questions.stem: Why may supplemental oxygen be needed during emergence from anesthesia?
options: Oxygen is required solely to speed anesthetic elimination
Residual anesthetic effects can depress ventilation and cause hypoxemia
questions.explanation: Residual anesthetic and sedative effects can depress ventilation as airway support is withdrawn. Supplemental oxygen may be needed, but it does not replace assessment of ventilation.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed p. 248; Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 11, printed p. 265

questions.stem: Assuming a PaCO₂–EtCO₂ gradient of 2–5 mmHg, what PaCO₂ is estimated when EtCO₂ is 28 mmHg?
questions.explanation: With an arterial-to-end-tidal gradient of 2–5 mmHg, an EtCO₂ of 28 estimates PaCO₂ at 30–33 mmHg. This is conditional because disease or perfusion changes can alter the gradient.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 18, printed p. 316

questions.stem: During laparoscopy, EtCO2 climbs from 35 to 48 mmHg. Which change addresses it?
questions.explanation: Absorbed insufflation CO₂ increases the amount the lungs must eliminate. Increasing effective minute ventilation addresses that load, with changes guided by monitoring and lung mechanics.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 34, printed pp. 809–810

questions.stem: Longer inspiratory time affects hemodynamics how?
questions.explanation: Longer positive intrathoracic pressure can reduce venous return. The resulting fall in preload may lower blood pressure, depending on volume status and ventilation settings.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 160

questions.stem: During exhalation, what drives gas out of the lungs?
options: Recoil of the lungs and chest wall
questions.explanation: Elastic recoil of the lungs and chest wall normally drives passive exhalation after inspiratory pressure is released. Expiratory muscle contraction or ventilator suction is not routinely required.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 152; Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 29, printed pp. 620–621

questions.stem: Why does bronchospasm require a longer expiratory time?
questions.explanation: Bronchospasm increases expiratory resistance and slows lung emptying. More expiratory time helps reduce trapped gas and intrinsic PEEP.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 29, printed p. 644

questions.stem: ARDS ventilation may use I:E ratios up to 1.5:1 to achieve what?
questions.explanation: Lengthening inspiration may raise mean airway pressure and recruit collapsed alveoli, improving oxygenation in selected patients. Inverse ratios carry air-trapping and hemodynamic risks and are not a universal ARDS target.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 159–160

questions.stem: A 170 cm man weighs 120 kg. Which weight sets his tidal volume?
questions.explanation: The cited protective-ventilation guidance bases tidal volume on ideal or predicted body weight. Obesity does not justify scaling tidal volume directly to actual body mass.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 277

questions.stem: Using a tidal-volume target of 6–8 mL/kg predicted body weight, what range corresponds to a 70-kg patient?
questions.explanation: Using 6–8 mL/kg predicted body weight gives 420–560 mL for 70 kg. This is a starting range under that strategy, adjusted for mechanics, pressures, and clinical need.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 159; Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 34, printed pp. 809–810

questions.stem: Set Vt 450 mL, circuit compliance 3 mL/cmH2O, PIP 30. Delivered Vt?
questions.explanation: If 30 cmH₂O is the pressure rise and compensation and fresh-gas contributions are absent, 3 × 30 = 90 mL is lost, leaving 360 mL. Baseline pressure and compensation are unspecified, so that result is conditional.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 4, printed p. 103; Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 152

questions.stem: Which intraoperative factor is highlighted as affecting delivered tidal volume?
questions.explanation: Some set volume compresses gas and expands compliant tubing rather than reaching the lungs. Circuit compliance therefore affects delivered volume unless the ventilator appropriately compensates.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 165

questions.stem: A patient on pressure support breathes rapidly and the ventilator auto-cycles with no visible effort. Which adjustment fits?
questions.explanation: Triggering without true patient effort suggests an overly responsive trigger or artifact. Make the trigger less responsive while checking for leaks or other artifacts; numerical sensitivity labels vary by ventilator.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 278

questions.stem: A weak patient can't trigger breaths on a −8 cmH2O pressure trigger. Which change helps?
options: Switch to a flow trigger around 2 L/min
questions.explanation: A weak patient needs assistance triggered by smaller inspiratory efforts rather than a more negative pressure threshold. A flow trigger may help, but the specified 2 L/min setting is device-dependent and unverified here.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 168; Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 278

questions.stem: After a recruitment maneuver, PEEP is set to 8 cmH2O and BP falls. Why?
options: PEEP improves preload and stroke volume
Less venous return from higher pressure
questions.explanation: PEEP increases intrathoracic pressure and can reduce venous return. Lower preload may therefore cause hypotension after recruitment or a PEEP increase.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 159, 164

questions.stem: PEEP should be titrated mainly to what?
questions.explanation: PEEP is adjusted to improve oxygenation while considering mechanics and hemodynamic tolerance. SpO₂ is useful but should be interpreted with the patient’s overall response.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 159, 164

questions.stem: An obese patient in steep Trendelenburg has a peak inspiratory pressure (PIP) of 32 cm H₂O. What is the best interpretation?
options: The pressure is too low, so tidal volume should be increased
The pressure alone proves a dangerous circuit obstruction
Assess plateau pressure, respiratory mechanics, and trends before judging safety
The pressure is normal for every healthy patient
questions.explanation: Obesity and steep Trendelenburg can reduce respiratory compliance and increase peak airway pressure. A single PIP does not establish safe alveolar pressure, so plateau pressure, tidal volume, and trends should also be evaluated.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 277

questions.stem: PIP rises sharply right after the patient is turned prone. Which cause should be considered first?
questions.explanation: Turning the patient can kink or displace the tracheal tube. A sudden pressure rise after positioning therefore warrants checking tube position and patency rather than assuming a leak or improved compliance.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 9, printed p. 232; Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 277

questions.stem: PIP rises after the surgeon leans on the chest. Which category is this?
questions.explanation: External chest compression makes the respiratory system harder to inflate. The text specifically lists a surgeon leaning on the chest as a cause of reduced compliance.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 29, printed p. 620

questions.stem: PIP drops when the patient goes from Trendelenburg to supine. Why?
questions.explanation: Returning from Trendelenburg to supine can improve respiratory-system compliance. At comparable volume and flow, less inflation pressure may then be required.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 277

questions.stem: Pplat is 32 cmH2O with PEEP 5. What is the best ventilator change?
questions.explanation: Plateau pressure reflects elastic loading plus PEEP during a no-flow hold. Reducing tidal volume lowers the elastic pressure requirement at unchanged compliance and is the pressure-reducing option listed here.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 152; Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 277

questions.stem: PIP 40, Pplat 18, PEEP 5. Which problem is most likely?
questions.explanation: The large difference between PIP and plateau pressure suggests a substantial resistive pressure component. High airway resistance therefore fits better than a new compliance problem under comparable flow conditions.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 152; Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 29, printed pp. 620–621

questions.stem: PIP 38, Pplat 34, PEEP 5. Which problem is most likely?
